Q: How to fix this python code to count different sized (length) samples in an image? A:

This isn't a complete answer - more of an extended comment with images to illustrate the way that I would be inclined to solve this problem. It is only effective for images that look like your example. This could be done on the original image but may be easier to handle if you first convolve with a suitable size disc with diameter chosen to make a nice clean white line down the middle of each rod.

Image after convolving with a disc - rods now appear solid with a thin white line down the middle. Compute the line description by fitting on that feature for each line between nodes. You might want to use a slightly smaller disc - the white lines don't really show up on SO.

Fit best fit lines to each linear feature using the same coordinate system (e.g. origin in one corner of the image). Then you can determine if a pair of line segments are in fact the same line relatively easily.

Use a greedy algorithm to take all the clean isolated rods out, followed by those with one crossing point, two crossing points etc until all segments are used up. I have colour coded the skeleton image according how the algorithm would proceed up to 4 crossings below.

Key red 0 nodes, orange 1 nodes, yellow 2 nodes, green 3 nodes, blue 4 nodes etc.

Colour coding the detections according to number of crossing nodes makes manual checking of the code much easier. If everything is in red then it is confusing.

I note that your code is ignoring short rods with a diameter to length ratio less than 6:1 is this intentional? It will seriously alter your statistics for the length distribution. There are quite a few of them not detected.

Q: arm64 Weak Memory Model: Why This assert(x == 1) Not Failing A:

The reason why you're not seeing different order of memory updates is because your two variables happen to be in the same cache line (by accident) and on arm the only misordered operations as far as I remember (it's been a few years) can only come from how cache is synchronized (other architectures can have store buffers and even cause ordering issues within the same cache line).

In your test code, change from:

volatile unsigned long x, y;

to:

volatile unsigned long v[256];

#define x v[0]
#define y v[64]

(also change the return type of main) and you'll start seeing what you expect to see:

% cc -std=c23 -o foo foo.c && ./foo
assert: x == 1 failed
assert: x == 1 failed
assert: x == 1 failed
assert: x == 1 failed
assert: x == 1 failed
^C
% uname -smv
Darwin Darwin Kernel Version 25.3.0: Wed Jan 28 20:54:55 PST 2026; root:xnu-12377.91.3~2/RELEASE_ARM64_T8132 arm64

change to #define y v[1] and run again and you'll see that the asserts go away again.

You can even experiment with the offset to experimentally find the cache line size on your CPU. I just used 64 because it would definitely be big enough for the foreseeable future.
